summary: The HTML format for RFCs relies on a Cascading Style Sheet specific to the RFC Series, which should account for accessibility and responsive design. This informational document describes the requirements for that default CSS.

eli5.summary: This lists what the style rules for the web version of an RFC need to do, like being readable on phones and for people who need accessibility help.

subtitle: What the default style sheet for the HTML version of RFCs must do, from fonts to printing.

tldr.problem: The HTML format for RFCs leaves all visual styling to one CSS, and that CSS needs agreed requirements so RFCs read well on any device.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets general requirements for layout, fonts, printing and lists, then says how specific CSS classes from RFC 7992 should look, such as pilcrows, compact lists and links.
tldr.outcome: It guides the RFC Editor's embedded default CSS, which readers can override locally. Later revisions were expected, and RFC 9920 updates it.

today: RFC 7993 is an Informational document from the IAB and has been updated by RFC 9920. It says its details were expected to change as the publishing tools were completed.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The HTML format in RFC 7992 leaves styling to a Cascading Style Sheet (CSS) defined for the RFC Series. That CSS is embedded in the published HTML and may be overridden by a local one. It is expected to take accessibility into account and follow a responsive design model.

This RFC states requirements for the default CSS used by the RFC Editor. Unless stated otherwise, styling must not alter the natural language content in any visible way. Many classes just mark elements semantically, so those elements should inherit their surrounding style. Some classes apply only to Internet-Drafts. The requirements apply only to HTML documents published by the RFC Editor as per RFC 7990, and the details are expected to change with experience.
sections.eli5: The web page of an RFC is styled by a set of look rules. This RFC lists what those rules must achieve so every reader gets a good page.

sections.title: Design Goal and General Requirements
sections.content:
The design goal is short: RFCs must be adaptable to a wide variety of devices and displays, accessible to assisted readers, and printable.

The general requirements are to support the semantic HTML of RFC 7992, to follow W3C best practice for accessibility and for mobile devices (the W3C's "Best Practices for Authoring HTML"), and to allow a broad range of internationalized scripts.
sections.eli5: The pages must work on big screens, small screens, screen readers and printers, and for many languages.

sections.title: Layout, Fonts, Printing and Lists
sections.content:
The document header must sit at the top and include what the RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322) and RFC 7841 describe. In the body, examples, code blocks and ASCII art must use a fixed-width font. Text must reflow as the screen shrinks, with a limited maximum width. Block quotes must be indented, tables must allow distinct header rows, and paragraphs should show a hover-over identifier. Links should be clearly distinguished, for example by color or text decoration.

For fonts, the default is a sans-serif family with broad Unicode support for browsers and a serif family for printing. Fonts should be publicly licensed and supported by all major browsers. The CSS must support printer-friendly output, with the print rules part of the embedded style sheet. Lists should have ample whitespace unless a compact class is used.
sections.eli5: Code has to be in letters that all have equal width, text has to shrink to fit a phone, links have to look like links, and the page has to print nicely.

sections.title: Specific CSS Classes
sections.content:
Section 7 walks through classes that change how content appears. Some examples:

  • .pilcrow appears at the end of a paragraph, artwork or sourcecode segment, stays hidden until moused over, does not print, and is not selected when copying.
  • .docInfo, .finalized and .rendered are hidden from visible content.
  • .dlCompact, .ulCompact and .olCompact use less spacing than the default.
  • .eref, .relref, .url and .xref must be clearly distinguished as links.
  • .cref, .crefAnchor and .crefSource are for comments in Internet-Drafts only and should be visually distinct.
  • .sourcecode uses a fixed-width font where one exists for the language.

Appendix A lists all classes. Apart from those in Section 7, none of them require specific changes to the content.
sections.eli5: Each kind of thing on the page has a name tag, like pilcrow or link. This part says how each one should look, such as hiding some, spacing lists out, or making links stand out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security vulnerabilities can be introduced through the CSS, as with CSS injection attacks. To avoid or mitigate attack vectors, the CSS used must comply with the current CSS specifications from the W3C.
sections.eli5: Even style rules can be misused by attackers, so the style sheet has to follow the official web rules carefully.
